--- title: "Choosing measures that match the objective" description: "The use the predictions are put to decides the measure. A shortlist of stations to revisit is scored on the animals it finds, which depend only on the order of the predictions, and a call at each station is scored on what its mistakes cost, which sets the threshold." order: 6 categories: [validation, metrics] --- {{< new-terms >}} ## The measure is chosen before any model is fitted [Regression performance measures](regression-metrics.qmd) and [Classification performance measures](classification-metrics.qmd) showed that measures can rank the same models in different orders. So the measure should be chosen before any model is fitted, from what the predictions will be used for. A map of abundance, a stock total, a list of stations to revisit and a decision at each station ask different things of a model, and a model that is best at one can be poor at another. This page sets out which measure suits which use, and adds two the earlier pages did not cover: the catch found by a shortlist, and the cost of the calls at a threshold chosen from what each mistake costs. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Each use has its own measure | The predictions are used for | Score them with | | --- | --- | | A map of abundance | the RMSE, aimed at the average count, and R² as `rsq_trad()` or `r2_score()` | | A total, such as a stock estimate | the predicted total over the observed one, beside the RMSE | | The typical station, where totals do not matter | MAE, aimed at the median | | A shortlist of the most promising stations | the animals the shortlist finds, against a perfect and a random shortlist | | A map of the chance of presence | log loss, with a calibration plot | | Comparing models before a threshold is chosen | ROC AUC | | A call at each station | the expected cost of the calls, at a threshold chosen from the costs; balanced accuracy or MCC while the costs are unknown | [Regression performance measures](regression-metrics.qmd) and [Classification performance measures](classification-metrics.qmd) showed why the first rows and the map of chances need their measures; this page adds the shortlist and the call at each station. A total alone is never enough: predicting the average gets the total right and says nothing about any station. None of these measures says whether an input causes what it predicts, which [Prediction and explanation](../01-introduction/prediction-and-explanation.qmd#test-error-cannot-reveal-a-confounder) showed a good predictor need not do. ## A shortlist is scored on what it finds Suppose a ship has time to revisit a fixed number of stations, its **budget**, and goes to the ones a model predicts the most animals at: a **shortlist**. The measure is the number of animals caught at those stations. Two benchmarks make it readable: a **perfect shortlist**, the stations that really held the most, and a random one, which finds the budget times the average catch. The shortlist depends only on the order of the predictions. Halving every prediction changes the RMSE and leaves the shortlist exactly as it was, so a model whose predictions run low, which the RMSE and R² punish, loses nothing here as long as it puts the stations in the right order. This is the same property as ROC AUC for presence, applied to a fixed number of stations. ## The costs of the two mistakes set the threshold [Class imbalance](../06-assumptions-limitations/class-imbalance.qmd#a-threshold-set-from-the-costs-does-the-work-of-rebalancing) said that the threshold should come from what each mistake costs. This can be made exact with the two mistakes of [Logistic regression](../03-supervised-learning/logistic-regression.qmd#the-threshold-trades-false-alarms-for-misses): a false alarm, a station called present where the species is absent, and a miss, a station called absent where it is present. If a false alarm costs $k$ times as much as a miss, the **expected cost** of the calls is $$ \text{expected cost} = \frac{\text{misses} + k \times \text{false alarms}}{\text{stations}}, $$ in units of one miss. A model that gives a station probability $p$ of presence expects a cost of $p$ from calling it absent and $k(1 - p)$ from calling it present. Calling it present is cheaper when $p$ is above $k/(1+k)$, so that is the threshold. When both mistakes cost the same, $k = 1$ and the threshold is the familiar 0.5; when a false alarm costs three times a miss, it is 0.75. ::: {.diagram} ![The threshold from the costs. Left, a false alarm costs three times a miss, and two stations are weighed: at a probability of presence of 0.6, calling it present expects a cost of 1.2 and calling it absent 0.6, so it is called absent; at 0.9, calling it present expects 0.3 and absent 0.9, so it is called present. Right, the threshold k over 1 plus k on the probability scale: 0.5 when the two mistakes cost the same, 0.75 when a false alarm costs three times a miss, 0.83 when it costs five times.](img/cost-threshold.svg){fig-alt="Two cards. Left, a false alarm costs 3 misses: for a station with probability 0.6, a bar for calling it present shows an expected cost of 3 times 0.4, which is 1.2, and a bar for calling it absent shows 0.6, so the cheaper call is absent. For a station with probability 0.9, calling it present costs 3 times 0.1, which is 0.3, and calling it absent costs 0.9, so the cheaper call is present. Right, the threshold is k over 1 plus k: an axis of probability of presence from 0 to 1, with three marks, 0.5 when k is 1, 0.75 when k is 3 and 0.83 when k is 5. Stations above the mark are called present. A note says the rule holds only when the probabilities are calibrated."} ::: The rule needs calibrated probabilities, as [Classification performance measures](classification-metrics.qmd#log-loss-rewards-probabilities-that-are-spread-out-and-calibrated) checked with a calibration plot. If a model's 0.8 does not mean 8 in 10, the cheapest threshold has to be found by working out the expected cost at every threshold instead. ## Worked example The shortlist is drawn from three of the models on [Regression performance measures](regression-metrics.qmd): **linear regression**, the **random forest**, and the **random forest on log counts**, whose predictions add up to well below the catch. The calls come from **logistic regression**, from [Classification performance measures](classification-metrics.qmd), whose probabilities were calibrated there. All four models are cross-validated on the same ten folds of sites as on those pages, so their out-of-fold predictions are the same. ### Preparing the data ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() |> mutate(log_abundance = log1p(abundance)) set.seed(61) folds <- group_vfold_cv(survey, group = site_id, v = 10) inputs <- c("depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu", "substrate", "season", "longitude", "latitude") with_inputs <- function(outcome, model) { recipe(reformulate(inputs, outcome), data = survey) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |> step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |> workflow(model) } forest <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |> set_engine("ranger", seed = 1) |> set_mode("regression") log_forest <- "Random forest on log counts" models <- list( "Linear regression" = with_inputs("abundance", linear_reg()), "Random forest" = with_inputs("abundance", forest), "Random forest on log counts" = with_inputs("log_abundance", forest) ) # every station's out-of-fold prediction from each model, in the survey's order out_of_fold <- map(models, \(model) { fit_resamples(model, folds, metrics = metric_set(rmse), control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE)) |> collect_predictions() |> arrange(.row) |> pull(.pred) }) # back from log counts to animals out_of_fold[[log_forest]] <- expm1(out_of_fold[[log_forest]]) caught <- survey$abundance tibble(stations = nrow(survey), `animals caught` = sum(caught), `average catch` = round(mean(caught), 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| stations| animals caught| average catch| |--------:|--------------:|-------------:| | 800| 3116| 3.9|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer, TransformedTargetRegressor from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, LogisticRegression from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold, cross_val_predict from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() caught = survey["abundance"].to_numpy() folds = GroupKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=61) inputs = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu", "substrate", "season", "longitude", "latitude"] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] numeric = [c for c in inputs if c not in categorical] def with_inputs(model): recipe = ColumnTransformer([ # scaling leaves an unpenalised fit unchanged and helps the solver ("numeric", Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("scale", StandardScaler())]), numeric), ("nominal", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", sparse_output=False), categorical), ]) return Pipeline([("recipe", recipe), ("model", model)]) # max_features="sqrt" draws a few inputs at each question, as ranger does. forest = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=500, max_features="sqrt", min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=1) models = { "Linear regression": LinearRegression(), "Random forest": forest, # fitted to log counts, each prediction turned back into animals "Random forest on log counts": TransformedTargetRegressor( forest, func=np.log1p, inverse_func=np.expm1), } # every station's out-of-fold prediction from each model, in the survey's order out_of_fold = {name: cross_val_predict(with_inputs(model), survey[inputs], caught, cv=folds, groups=survey["site_id"]) for name, model in models.items()} pd.DataFrame({"stations": [len(survey)], "animals caught": [caught.sum()], "average catch": [round(caught.mean(), 2)]}) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | stations | animals caught | average catch | |-----------:|-----------------:|----------------:| | 800 | 3116 | 3.9 | ::: ::: ::: ### Predictions that run low lose nothing on a shortlist The ship has time for 100 of the 800 stations. The table sets each model's shortlist beside its RMSE and its predicted total. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} budget <- 100 # the animals caught at the stations a set of predictions ranks highest found_by <- function(predicted) { sum(caught[order(predicted, decreasing = TRUE)][seq_len(budget)]) } perfect <- sum(sort(caught, decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(budget)]) at_random <- budget * mean(caught) shortlists <- tibble( model = names(out_of_fold), RMSE = map_dbl(out_of_fold, \(predicted) rmse_vec(caught, predicted)), `predicted / caught` = map_dbl(out_of_fold, \(predicted) sum(predicted) / sum(caught)), `animals found` = map_dbl(out_of_fold, found_by), `share of a perfect shortlist` = `animals found` / perfect ) shortlists |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|model | RMSE| predicted / caught| animals found| share of a perfect shortlist| |:---------------------------|----:|------------------:|-------------:|----------------------------:| |Linear regression | 4.39| 1.00| 860| 0.63| |Random forest | 4.32| 1.04| 784| 0.57| |Random forest on log counts | 4.47| 0.69| 847| 0.62|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} budget = 100 # the animals caught at the stations a set of predictions ranks highest def found_by(predicted): return caught[np.argsort(-predicted, kind="stable")][:budget].sum() perfect = np.sort(caught)[::-1][:budget].sum() at_random = budget * caught.mean() shortlists = pd.DataFrame([ {"model": name, "RMSE": root_mean_squared_error(caught, predicted), "predicted / caught": predicted.sum() / caught.sum(), "animals found": found_by(predicted), "share of a perfect shortlist": found_by(predicted) / perfect} for name, predicted in out_of_fold.items()]) shortlists.round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | model | RMSE | predicted / caught | animals found | share of a perfect shortlist | |:----------------------------|-------:|---------------------:|----------------:|-------------------------------:| | Linear regression | 4.39 | 0.99 | 864 | 0.63 | | Random forest | 4.25 | 0.99 | 798 | 0.58 | | Random forest on log counts | 4.5 | 0.66 | 789 | 0.58 | ::: ::: ::: A perfect shortlist of 100 stations would find 1,367 animals, and 100 stations chosen at random about 390. The forest on log counts has the highest RMSE of the three, 4.47, and predicts only 69% of the animals caught. Its shortlist finds 847 animals, against 784 for the same forest fitted to the counts and 860 for linear regression. Its predictions run low, but in much the same order, and the order is all a shortlist uses. The gaps between the three are small. The Python tab, with its own folds and forests, puts them in another order, and [Uncertainty and stability](uncertainty-and-stability.qmd) showed that gaps this size need a paired comparison before they count as a ranking. The result shared by all three is plainer: each shortlist finds about 61% of what a perfect one would, and 2.1 times what a random one finds. A sentence such as "revisiting the 100 stations this model ranks highest should find about 2.1 times as many animals as 100 stations chosen at random" tells a survey planner more than an RMSE does. ### The cheapest threshold follows the cost of a false alarm Suppose every station called present is visited by a dive team. A false alarm wastes a dive; a miss leaves a station with the species out of the record. The expected cost is worked out at every threshold from 0.01 to 0.99, for false alarms that cost one, three and five times as much as a miss. The last column is the cheaper of two rules that need no model: call every station present, or call none. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # logistic regression's out-of-fold probability of presence, in the survey's order probability <- fit_resamples(with_inputs("present", logistic_reg()), folds, metrics = metric_set(roc_auc), control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE)) |> collect_predictions() |> arrange(.row) |> pull(.pred_yes) present <- survey$present == "yes" expected_cost <- function(threshold, k) { called <- probability >= threshold (sum(!called & present) + k * sum(called & !present)) / length(present) } cost_curves <- expand_grid(k = c(1, 3, 5), threshold = seq(0.01, 0.99, by = 0.01)) |> mutate(cost = map2_dbl(threshold, k, expected_cost)) cheapest <- cost_curves |> slice_min(cost, by = k, with_ties = FALSE) |> mutate(`k / (1 + k)` = k / (1 + k), `stations called present` = map_int(threshold, \(t) sum(probability >= t)), `cost at 0.5` = map_dbl(k, \(k) expected_cost(0.5, k)), # calling every station present, or none `cost without the model` = pmin(k * mean(!present), mean(present))) |> select(k, `k / (1 + k)`, `cheapest threshold` = threshold, `stations called present`, `cost there` = cost, `cost at 0.5`, `cost without the model`) cheapest |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| k| k / (1 + k)| cheapest threshold| stations called present| cost there| cost at 0.5| cost without the model| |--:|-----------:|------------------:|-----------------------:|----------:|-----------:|----------------------:| | 1| 0.500| 0.51| 773| 0.214| 0.218| 0.225| | 3| 0.750| 0.75| 489| 0.534| 0.635| 0.675| | 5| 0.833| 0.83| 343| 0.639| 1.052| 0.775|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} # logistic regression's out-of-fold probability of presence, in the survey's order; # column 1 of predict_proba is the probability of True present = (survey["present"] == "yes").to_numpy() probability = cross_val_predict( with_inputs(LogisticRegression(C=np.inf, max_iter=5000)), survey[inputs], present, cv=folds, groups=survey["site_id"], method="predict_proba")[:, 1] def expected_cost(threshold, k): called = probability >= threshold return (np.sum(~called & present) + k * np.sum(called & ~present)) / len(present) thresholds = np.round(np.arange(0.01, 0.995, 0.01), 2) def cheapest_for(k): costs = np.array([expected_cost(t, k) for t in thresholds]) best = thresholds[np.argmin(costs)] return {"k": k, "k / (1 + k)": k / (1 + k), "cheapest threshold": best, "stations called present": int(np.sum(probability >= best)), "cost there": costs.min(), "cost at 0.5": expected_cost(0.5, k), # calling every station present, or none "cost without the model": min(k * np.mean(~present), np.mean(present))} cheapest = pd.DataFrame([cheapest_for(k) for k in (1, 3, 5)]) cheapest.round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | k | k / (1 + k) | cheapest threshold | stations called present | cost there | cost at 0.5 | cost without the model | |----:|--------------:|---------------------:|--------------------------:|-------------:|--------------:|-------------------------:| | 1 | 0.5 | 0.48 | 789 | 0.219 | 0.222 | 0.225 | | 3 | 0.75 | 0.79 | 421 | 0.554 | 0.642 | 0.675 | | 5 | 0.833 | 0.85 | 289 | 0.676 | 1.062 | 0.775 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} panels <- transmute(cheapest, k, panel = sprintf( "A false alarm costs %g %s\ncheapest at %.2f", k, if_else(k == 1, "miss", "misses"), `cheapest threshold`)) cost_curves <- cost_curves |> left_join(panels, by = "k") |> mutate(panel = fct_inorder(panel)) at_cheapest <- semi_join(cost_curves, cheapest, by = c("k", "threshold" = "cheapest threshold")) without_model <- left_join(cheapest, panels, by = "k") ggplot(cost_curves, aes(threshold, cost, colour = panel)) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, colour = "grey70", linetype = "dashed") + geom_hline(data = without_model, aes(yintercept = `cost without the model`), colour = "grey45", linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 0.8) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(data = at_cheapest, size = 3) + facet_wrap(~panel, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") + scale_colour_ml() + labs(x = "Threshold", y = "Expected cost\n(misses per station)") + theme(legend.position = "none") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Expected cost of logistic regression's calls at every threshold, in units of one miss, when a false alarm costs one, three and five times as much as a miss. The point marks the cheapest threshold, named above each panel, the dashed line 0.5, and the dotted line the cost without the model. The cheapest threshold moves from 0.51 to 0.83 as false alarms get dearer, close to k/(1 + k) each time.](choosing-a-metric_files/figure-html/fig-cost-1.png){#fig-cost fig-alt='Three panels side by side, for a false alarm costing 1, 3 and 5 misses, each with the threshold from 0 to 1 along the bottom and the expected cost per station up the side, a dashed vertical line at 0.5 and a dotted horizontal line for the cost without the model. Each curve has a marked lowest point, at 0.51 when the two mistakes cost the same, 0.75 when a false alarm costs 3 misses and 0.83 when it costs 5, each a little below the dotted line. In the five-times panel the curve at 0.5 is 1.05, far above the dotted line at 0.78.' width=1700} ::: ::: ::: The cheapest thresholds are 0.51, 0.75 and 0.83, against 0.50, 0.75 and 0.83 from the rule: logistic regression's probabilities are calibrated well enough for the rule to work. When a false alarm costs five misses, the cheapest threshold calls 343 of the 800 stations present, and leaving the threshold at 0.5 costs 1.65 times as much. The model is the same in every panel; only the threshold has changed. The rules without a model are hard to beat here, because the species was caught at 78% of the stations. At five to one, a threshold of 0.5 costs 1.05 per station, more than the 0.78 of calling no station present at all. The cheapest threshold costs 0.64, a saving of 18% on that rule. A model is worth using only at a threshold that suits the costs, and only if it beats the rules that need none. ## The report states what the measure assumes A measure carries assumptions, and the report should state them. A shortlist measure assumes a budget, and the order of the models can change with it, so compute it at the budget the survey really has. A threshold assumes a ratio of costs. Leaving it at 0.5 assumes that a false alarm and a miss cost the same, which is rarely true and rarely written down. "Stations above 0.75 were called present, as a wasted dive costs about three times a missed record" is a sentence a reader can check, and one that lets someone with other costs reuse the model. Every measure in this section compares predictions with what the survey recorded. If the records themselves are biased, by the gear, the observers or where the effort went, a model that matches them well matches the bias too, and no measure can show it. [From a model to a claim](../10-interpretation/from-model-to-claim.qmd) shows such a gear on the survey. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - Choose the measure from the use of the predictions, before fitting: a map, a total, a shortlist, a map of chances, or a call at each station. - A **shortlist** is scored on the animals it finds, against a perfect and a random one. It depends only on the order of the predictions: the forest on log counts predicted 69% of the catch, yet its shortlist of 100 stations found about as many animals as the other models'. - The **expected cost** of the calls counts misses and false alarms by what each costs. If a false alarm costs $k$ misses, calibrated probabilities are cheapest at a threshold of $k/(1+k)$. - For logistic regression the cheapest thresholds fell at 0.51, 0.75 and 0.83. At five to one, a threshold of 0.5 cost more than calling no station present at all. - State the budget and the cost ratio behind a measure. A threshold of 0.5 assumes the two mistakes cost the same. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Work out the shortlists for budgets of 50 and 200 stations. Does the same model find the most animals at every budget? 2. Use the random forest's probabilities of presence from [Classification performance measures](classification-metrics.qmd) in place of logistic regression's. Do the cheapest thresholds still fall at $k/(1+k)$?
